items.title: 4.2 Work done by a variable force

source_refs.note: Topic 4.2 with Figs. 4.5 to 4.8 and Example 4.1 (PDF 76-78, printed 73-75).

blocks.text: In many cases the force does not remain constant during the process of doing work. For example, as a rocket moves away from the Earth, work is done against the force of gravity, which varies as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre; similarly the force exerted by a spring increases with the amount of stretch. How can we calculate the work done in such situations?

Fig. 4.5 shows the path of a particle in the xy-plane as it moves from point P to point Q. The path is divided into n short intervals of displacements delta d1, delta d2, ..., delta dn, and F1, F2, ..., Fn are the forces acting during these intervals. During each small interval the force is supposed to be approximately constant, so the work done for the first interval is delta W1 = F1 . delta d1 = F1 cos theta1 delta d1, and in the second interval delta W2 = F2 . delta d2 = F2 cos theta2 delta d2, and so on. The total work done in moving the object is found by adding all these terms: W_total = delta W1 + delta W2 + ... + delta Wn = F1 cos theta1 delta d1 + F2 cos theta2 delta d2 + ... + Fn cos thetan delta dn, or W_total = sum from i = 1 to n of F_i cos theta_i delta d_i ... (4.4).

blocks.alt: A curved path from point P up to point Q is cut by tick marks into short intervals delta d1, delta d2 ... delta dn. Force F1 acts at P at an angle theta1 to the path, and force F2 acts at the start of the second interval at an angle theta2.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.5: A particle acted upon by a variable force, moves along the path shown from point P to point Q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.5).

blocks.text: This can be examined graphically by plotting F cos theta against d (Fig. 4.6), with the displacement d sub-divided into the same n equal intervals and the value of F cos theta at the beginning of each interval indicated. The i-th shaded rectangle has area F_i cos theta_i delta d_i, the work done during the i-th interval; so the work given by Eq. 4.4 equals the sum of the areas of all the rectangles. If we sub-divide the distance into a large number of intervals so that each delta d becomes very small, the work given by Eq. 4.4 becomes more accurate, and letting each delta d approach zero gives an exact result: W_total = limit (delta d -> 0) of the sum from i = 1 to n of F_i cos theta_i delta d_i ... (4.5).

blocks.alt: A graph of F cos theta against d with origin O and axes x and y. From P to Q the displacement is divided into equal intervals delta d1, delta d2 ... delta di ... delta dn. Each shaded strip has the height of F cos theta at the beginning of its interval, marked F1 cos theta1, Fi cos theta i and Fn cos theta n; the smooth curve runs over them.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.6: F cos theta against d, divided into n equal intervals (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.6).

blocks.text: In this limit the total area of the rectangles (Fig. 4.6) approaches the area between the F cos theta against d curve and the x-axis from P to Q (Fig. 4.7).

blocks.alt: A graph of F cos theta against Displacement d with origin O. The whole region under the smooth curve between P and Q is shaded, with dashed vertical lines at P and Q.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.7: The area under the F cos theta against d curve between P and Q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.7).

blocks.title: Work by a variable force
blocks.text: The work done by a variable force in moving a particle between two points is equal to the area under the F cos theta against d curve between the two points P and Q (Fig. 4.7).

blocks.title: Example 4.1
blocks.text: A force F acting on an object varies with distance d as shown in Fig. 4.8 (5 N from d = 0 to d = 4 m, then falling linearly to zero at d = 6 m). Calculate the work done by the force as the object moves from d = 0 to d = 6 m. Solution: the work done equals the total area under the curve from d = 0 to d = 6 m, which is the area of the rectangular section from d = 0 to d = 4 m plus the area of the triangular section from d = 4 m to d = 6 m. Work represented by the rectangle = 4 m x 5 N = 20 N m = 20 J; work represented by the triangle = (1/2) x 2 m x 5 N = 5 N m = 5 J. Therefore the total work done = 20 J + 5 J = 25 J.

blocks.alt: A graph of F in newtons (0 to 5) against d in metres (0 to 6). The force is 5 N from d = 0 to d = 4 m, then falls in a straight line to zero at d = 6 m. The rectangle from 0 to 4 m and the triangle from 4 to 6 m under the graph are shaded in two colours.
